claim: Eukaryotic ribosomes consist of a small (40S) and a large (60S) subunit that are comprised of four ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) and 79–80 ribosomal proteins.
source: Eukaryotic ribosomes consist of a small (40S) and a large (60S) subunit that are comprised of four ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) and 79–80 ribosomal proteins.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of molecular biology, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: The yeast 40S subunit contains the 18S rRNA and 33 ribosomal proteins.
source: While the yeast 40S subunit contains the 18S rRNA and 33 ribosomal proteins, the 60S subunit contains the 5S, 5.8S, and 25S rRNA species and 46 ribosomal proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast ribosome composition.

claim: The yeast 60S subunit contains the 5S, 5.8S, and 25S rRNA species and 46 ribosomal proteins.
source: While the yeast 40S subunit contains the 18S rRNA and 33 ribosomal proteins, the 60S subunit contains the 5S, 5.8S, and 25S rRNA species and 46 ribosomal proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast ribosome composition.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis starts in the nucleolus by transcription of a common precursor RNA (the 35S pre-rRNA) and the co-transcriptional association of the first ribosomal proteins and assembly factors.
source: The two ribosomal subunits are assembled in a complex highly regulated and hierarchical biogenesis process that starts in the nucleolus by transcription of a common precursor RNA (the 35S pre-rRNA) and the co-transcriptional association of the first ribosomal proteins and assembly factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome biogenesis, supported by citations to review articles (Baßler and Hurt, 2019; de la Cruz et al., 2015; Klinge and Woolford, 2019; Kressler et al., 2017).

claim: Upon endonucleolytic cleavage within the internal RNA spacer element 1 (ITS1), the pre-40S and pre-60S subunits follow separate biogenesis routes in the nucleolus, nucleoplasm, and finally cytoplasm.
source: Upon endonucleolytic cleavage within the internal RNA spacer element 1 (ITS1), the pre-40S and pre-60S subunits follow separate biogenesis routes in the nucleolus, nucleoplasm, and finally cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome biogenesis pathways, supported by review citations.

claim: The 25S rRNA contains six intertwined domains named in the 5' to 3' direction as domains I to VI.
source: The precursors of the large ribosomal subunit undergo a cascade of consecutive rRNA folding steps in which the initially flexible six intertwined 25S rRNA domains (named in the 5' to 3' direction as domains I to VI) get integrated into the developing 60S core.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rRNA structure.

claim: In the earliest precursors the 27SA2 pre-rRNA is highly flexible.
source: While in the earliest precursors the 27SA2 pre-rRNA is highly flexible, the proportion of stably folded rRNA domains is strongly increased in succeeding 27SB pre-rRNA containing precursor particles (Burlacu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burlacu et al., 2017.

claim: The proportion of stably folded rRNA domains is strongly increased in 27SB pre-rRNA containing precursor particles.
source: While in the earliest precursors the 27SA2 pre-rRNA is highly flexible, the proportion of stably folded rRNA domains is strongly increased in succeeding 27SB pre-rRNA containing precursor particles (Burlacu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burlacu et al., 2017.

claim: Cryo-EM structures revealed that shaping of the immature rRNA occurs in a hierarchical order.
source: In line with chemical probing data, cryo-EM structures revealed that shaping of the immature rRNA occurs in a hierarchical order, in which first the 25S rRNA domains I, II, and parts of domain VI, together with the 5.8S rRNA and internal transcribed spacer 2 (ITS2), adopt a folded conformation and form the solvent-exposed back side of the pre-60S particle (structural states 1/A and 2/B) (Kater et al., 2017; Sanghai et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cryo-EM structural studies (Kater et al., 2017; Sanghai et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2019b).

claim: In structural states 1/A and 2/B, the 25S rRNA domains I, II, and parts of domain VI, together with the 5.8S rRNA and ITS2, adopt a folded conformation and form the solvent-exposed back side of the pre-60S particle.
source: In line with chemical probing data, cryo-EM structures revealed that shaping of the immature rRNA occurs in a hierarchical order, in which first the 25S rRNA domains I, II, and parts of domain VI, together with the 5.8S rRNA and internal transcribed spacer 2 (ITS2), adopt a folded conformation and form the solvent-exposed back side of the pre-60S particle (structural states 1/A and 2/B) (Kater et al., 2017; Sanghai et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cryo-EM structural studies.

claim: Compaction of large parts of domains III, IV, and V results in formation of the polypeptide exit tunnel (PET) in state C to E particles.
source: Subsequent compaction of large parts of domains III, IV, and V results in formation of the polypeptide exit tunnel (PET) in state C to E particles.
evidence: This is a description of structural maturation stages based on cryo-EM studies.

claim: Transition of the 60S precursors to the nucleoplasm goes along with a re-positioning of the L1 stalk (helices H75-H78 of 25S rRNA domain V).
source: Transition of the 60S precursors to the nucleoplasm goes along with a re-positioning of the L1 stalk (helices H75-H78 of 25S rRNA domain V) allowing restructuring and incorporation of large parts of domain V and formation of the central-protuberance (CP) (state F/Nog2 particles) (Kater et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies (Kater et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2016).

claim: The 5S rRNA is transcribed independently from the other rRNA species.
source: As part of the CP, the 5S rRNA, which is transcribed independently from the other rRNA species and flexibly assembled at an earlier maturation stage, becomes stably integrated and structurally visible at this stage (Leidig et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about 5S rRNA biogenesis, supported by citations.

claim: The 5S rRNA becomes stably integrated and structurally visible at the state F/Nog2 particle stage.
source: As part of the CP, the 5S rRNA, which is transcribed independently from the other rRNA species and flexibly assembled at an earlier maturation stage, becomes stably integrated and structurally visible at this stage (Leidig et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies (Leidig et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2016).

claim: Upon removal of ITS2 and rotational movement of the 5S rRNA into its nearly mature orientation, the pre-60S intermediates are exported to the cytoplasm.
source: Upon subsequent removal of ITS2 and rotational movement of the 5S rRNA into its nearly mature orientation, the pre-60S intermediates are exported to the cytoplasm (Gasse et al., 2015; Kater et al., 2020; Matsuo et al., 2014; Schuller et al., 2018; Thoms et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural and functional studies.

claim: Final structuring of the inter-subunit side (ISS) and the peptidyl-transferase centre (PTC) completes 60S maturation in the cytoplasm.
source: Here, final structuring of the inter-subunit side (ISS) and the peptidyl-transferase centre (PTC) completes 60S maturation and permits entrance of the assembled subunit to the pool of actively translating ribosomes (Kargas et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2017; Malyutin et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Ribosome assembly requires ca. 80 small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) and at least 200 non-ribosomal assembly factors.
source: The accurate and efficient rRNA maturation and ribosome assembly requires ca. 80 small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) and at least 200 non-ribosomal assembly factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the complexity of ribosome biogenesis.

claim: Among ribosome assembly factors are a variety of energy consuming enzymes such as AAA+-ATPases and RNA helicases that facilitate key RNA and protein remodelling events on nascent ribosomal intermediates.
source: Among these assembly factors are a variety of energy consuming enzymes such as AAA+-ATPases and RNA helicases that facilitate key RNA and protein remodelling events on nascent ribosomal intermediates (Kressler et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kressler et al., 2010.

claim: The activity of the dynein-related AAA+-ATPase Rea1 is required for two separate ATP-hydrolysis-dependent pre-60S maturation steps.
source: The activity of the dynein-related AAA+-ATPase Rea1 is required for two separate ATP-hydrolysis-dependent pre-60S maturation steps.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent detailed descriptions and citations.

claim: Rea1 releases assembly factor Ytm1 and its binding partner Erb1 from late nucleolar pre-60S particles.
source: In the earlier step, Rea1 releases assembly factor Ytm1 and its binding partner Erb1 from late nucleolar pre-60S particles (Bassler et al., 2010; Thoms et al., 2016; Wegrecki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Bassler et al., 2010; Thoms et al., 2016; Wegrecki et al., 2015).

claim: Rea1 dislodges assembly factor Rsa4 during CP formation in the nucleoplasm, thereby priming the 60S precursors for their export to the cytoplasm.
source: In a second maturation step, which goes along with CP formation in the nucleoplasm, Rea1 dislodges assembly factor Rsa4 and thereby primes the 60S precursors for their export to the cytoplasm (Barrio-Garcia et al., 2016; Kater et al., 2020; Matsuo et al., 2014; Ulbrich et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The interaction of Rea1 with Ytm1 and Rsa4 is established between a metal-ion-dependent adhesion site (MIDAS) at the C-terminal tip of the Rea1 tail and the ubiquitin-like (UBL) domains of its assembly factor ligands.
source: The interaction of Rea1 with Ytm1 and Rsa4 is established between a metal-ion-dependent adhesion site (MIDAS) at the C-terminal tip of the Rea1 tail and the ubiquitin-like (UBL) domains of its assembly factor ligands (Ahmed et al., 2019; Bassler et al., 2010; Mickolajczyk et al., 2022; Ulbrich et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The pentameric Rix1-complex serves as docking platform for Rea1 on nucleoplasmic pre-60S particles.
source: We previously revealed the architecture of Rea1 and its associated pentameric Rix1-complex, which serves as docking platform for the ATPase on nucleoplasmic pre-60S particles (Barrio-Garcia et al., 2016; Kater et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies by the authors.

claim: A highly conserved loop motif within the Rea1 MIDAS facilitates the attachment of the C-terminal MIDAS onto the N-terminal AAA+ ring domain upon pre-60S association.
source: Upon pre-60S association, a highly conserved loop motif within the Rea1 MIDAS facilitates the attachment of the C-terminal MIDAS onto the N-terminal AAA+ ring domain (Ahmed et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2018; Kater et al., 2020; Sosnowski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Intramolecular MIDAS docking may enable a direct force-transmission upon ATP hydrolysis from the AAA+ domain onto the MIDAS to dislodge the MIDAS-bound Rsa4 ligand.
source: This intramolecular MIDAS docking may enable a direct force-transmission upon ATP hydrolysis from the AAA+ domain onto the MIDAS to dislodge the MIDAS-bound Rsa4 ligand.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: Inhibition of Ytm1 release resulted in a shift of otherwise nucleoplasmic Rix1 particles to a nucleolar stage.
source: While there is no direct evidence that the Rix1-complex recruits Rea1 also to nucleolar 60S precursors, inhibition of Ytm1 release resulted in a shift of otherwise nucleoplasmic Rix1 particles to a nucleolar stage (Bassler et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bassler et al., 2010.

claim: Around 20 RNA helicases involved in ribosome biogenesis have been identified.
source: Around 20 RNA helicases involved in ribosome biogenesis have been identified so far (Granneman et al., 2006; Mitterer and Pertschy, 2022; Rodríguez-Galán et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The DEAD-box helicase Spb4 is essential for cell viability and 60S assembly.
source: The DEAD-box helicase Spb4 is essential for cell viability and 60S assembly (de la Cruz et al., 1998; García-Gómez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spb4 exhibits RNA-stimulated ATPase activity in vitro.
source: Spb4 exhibits RNA-stimulated ATPase activity in vitro, which is abolished by a point mutation within the catalytic DEAD (Walker B) helicase motif (Brüning et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brüning et al., 2018.

claim: Upon Spb4 depletion and in spb4 catalytic mutant backgrounds, processing of the 27SB pre-rRNA on pre-60S particles was blocked.
source: Upon its depletion and in spb4 catalytic mutant backgrounds, processing of the 27SB pre-rRNA on pre-60S particles was blocked (Brüning et al., 2018; de la Cruz et al., 1998; García-Gómez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depletion of Spb4 impaired the recruitment of the late B-factor Nog2, which is necessary for subsequent 27SB processing.
source: In line with this, depletion of Spb4 impaired the recruitment of the late B-factor Nog2, which is necessary for subsequent 27SB processing (Talkish et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Talkish et al., 2012.

claim: Low-resolution cryo-EM density and CRAC experiments suggested that Spb4 binds to pre-60S intermediates at a hinge region at the base of eukaryote-specific expansion segment 27 (ES27) within 25S rRNA domain IV.
source: A low-resolution cryo-EM density and CRAC (UV-crosslinking and cDNA analysis) experiments suggested that Spb4 binds to pre-60S intermediates at a hinge region at the base of eukaryote-specific expansion segment 27 (ES27) within 25S rRNA domain IV (Brüning et al., 2018; Kater et al., 2017; Sanghai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and crosslinking studies.

claim: Spb4 and Rrp17 bind to pre-60S intermediates directly prior to their transition to the nucleoplasm, which is mediated by the Rea1 AAA+-ATPase.
source: Here, we report an essential function of the RNA helicase Spb4 and its interaction partner Rrp17 for the maturation of late nucleolar pre-60S particles. Spb4 and Rrp17 bind to such intermediates directly prior to their transition to the nucleoplasm, which is mediated by the Rea1 AAA+-ATPase.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of Spb4 bound to pre-60S particles suggests how the helicase facilitates restructuring of its substrate rRNA before it can later fold into its mature-like conformation.
source: Consistent with a most recently published study (Cruz et al., 2022), our cryo-EM structure of Spb4 bound to pre-60S particles suggests how the helicase facilitates restructuring of its substrate rRNA before it can later fold into its mature-like conformation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by cryo-EM structural data and consistent with a recent publication.

claim: The association of Spb4 with 60S precursors is required to allow the Rea1-dependent release of the Ytm1–Erb1 subcomplex.
source: Furthermore, the association of Spb4 with 60S precursors is required to allow the Rea1-dependent release of the Ytm1–Erb1 subcomplex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by in vitro maturation assays.

claim: Spb4 and Rrp17 were accumulated on pre-60S particles isolated via Ytm1 E80A but not via wild-type Ytm1.
source: Consistent with this observation, Spb4 was enriched on pre-60S particles isolated via Ytm1 E80A but not via wild-type Ytm1, whereas earlier nucleolar assembly factors (e.g. Noc1, Rrp5, Drs1) already dissociated at this stage (Figure 1A; Kater et al., 2017). Besides Spb4, another assembly factor, Rrp17, was accumulated on these Ytm1 E80A particles (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Spb4 and Rrp17 have a function during late steps of nucleolar pre-60S maturation.
source: Besides Spb4, another assembly factor, Rrp17, was accumulated on these Ytm1 E80A particles (Figure 1A), indicating that both, Spb4 and Rrp17, have a function during late steps of nucleolar pre-60S maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation pattern observed in the experiments.

claim: Auxin-induced depletion of Spb4-HA-AID and Rrp17-HA-AID yielded non-viable yeast cells.
source: As previous studies suggested a role of the SPB4 and RRP17 genes in ribosome biogenesis (Brüning et al., 2018; de la Cruz et al., 1998; García-Gómez et al., 2011; Oeffinger et al., 2009), we tested their essential functions by depletion of the Spb4-HA-AID and Rrp17-HA-AID proteins via an auxin-inducible degron (AID) approach, which as anticipated yielded non-viable yeast cells (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Point mutations of the catalytic helicase core domains (K57R, E173A, R360A) in Spb4 were lethal or exhibited a slow-growth phenotype.
source: Moreover, we analysed spb4 point mutations of the catalytic helicase core domains (K57R: ATP-binding motif, E173A: ATP-hydrolysis motif, R360A: ATP-hydrolysis motif), and Spb4 C-terminal truncation mutants, which turned out to be lethal or exhibited a slow-growth phenotype (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Spb4 C-terminal truncation mutants were lethal or exhibited a slow-growth phenotype.
source: Moreover, we analysed spb4 point mutations of the catalytic helicase core domains (K57R: ATP-binding motif, E173A: ATP-hydrolysis motif, R360A: ATP-hydrolysis motif), and Spb4 C-terminal truncation mutants, which turned out to be lethal or exhibited a slow-growth phenotype (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Spb4 helicase mutants and C-terminal truncations still co-purify pre-ribosomal particles, however, somewhat less efficiently.
source: Subsequent affinity purifications of the helicase mutants and the C-terminal Spb4 truncations, all tagged with Flag-TEV-protein A (FTpA), showed that they still co-purify pre-ribosomal particles, however, somewhat less efficiently (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The C-terminal domain (CTD) of Spb4 has an essential pre-60S targeting function.
source: This indicates an essential pre-60S targeting function of the C-terminal domain (CTD), which was recently described also for DDX55, the human homologue of Spb4 (Choudhury et al., 2021), whereas another recent study on yeast Spb4 suggested that not the entire CTD is strictly required for pre-60S assembly (Cruz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The Spb4 function on nascent 60S pre-ribosomes depends on both the catalytic and C-terminal domain.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that the Spb4 function on nascent 60S pre-ribosomes depends on both the catalytic and C-terminal domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on mutants.

claim: Affinity purifications via wild-type Spb4 co-enriched a pattern of assembly factors highly similar to Ytm1 E80A particles (state E) and contained large amounts of Rrp17.
source: In contrast to the tested spb4 mutants, affinity purifications via wild-type Spb4 co-enriched a pattern of assembly factors highly similar to Ytm1 E80A particles (state E) and contained large amounts of Rrp17 (Figure 1D, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Rrp17-FTpA affinity purifications co-enriched pre-60S particles with a comparable assembly factor composition to Spb4 purifications and also contained downstream nucleoplasmic assembly factors like Nog2, Rsa4, and Nop53.
source: Vice versa, Rrp17-FTpA affinity purifications co-enriched pre-60S particles with a comparable assembly factor composition and Spb4 but in contrast to Spb4 purifications also a few downstream nucleoplasmic assembly factors like Nog2, Rsa4, and the ITS2 foot-factor Nop53 (Figure 1D, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both Spb4 and Rrp17 join the maturation pathway around nucleolar state E.
source: Based on these affinity purifications, we conclude that both, Spb4 and Rrp17, join the maturation pathway around nucleolar state E.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the affinity purification data.

claim: Spb4 dissociates during or shortly after release of Ytm1–Erb1 by Rea1.
source: While Spb4 subsequently dissociates during or shortly after release of Ytm1–Erb1 by Rea1, Rrp17 may remain associated on downstream intermediates upon Nop53 association (Nop53 binds pre-60S particles at state NE1 upon Ytm1–Erb1 removal).
evidence: This is inferred from the affinity purification data showing different assembly factor compositions.

claim: Rrp17 may remain associated on downstream intermediates upon Nop53 association.
source: While Spb4 subsequently dissociates during or shortly after release of Ytm1–Erb1 by Rea1, Rrp17 may remain associated on downstream intermediates upon Nop53 association (Nop53 binds pre-60S particles at state NE1 upon Ytm1–Erb1 removal).
evidence: This is inferred from the affinity purification data.

claim: In the absence of Spb4 or Rrp17, pre-60S maturation was effectively arrested at a late nucleolar stage.
source: In the absence of Spb4 or Rrp17, pre-60S maturation was effectively arrested at a late nucleolar stage, as apparent by the accumulation of assembly factors Ytm1–Erb1, Spb1, and Has1 on Nug1- and Nop7-derived particles, whereas the recruitment of Nop53 and downstream nucleoplasmic assembly factors such as Nog2 and Bud20 to these stalled maturation intermediates was impaired (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Upon Spb4 or Rrp17 depletion, assembly factors Ytm1–Erb1, Spb1, and Has1 accumulated on Nug1- and Nop7-derived particles.
source: In the absence of Spb4 or Rrp17, pre-60S maturation was effectively arrested at a late nucleolar stage, as apparent by the accumulation of assembly factors Ytm1–Erb1, Spb1, and Has1 on Nug1- and Nop7-derived particles, whereas the recruitment of Nop53 and downstream nucleoplasmic assembly factors such as Nog2 and Bud20 to these stalled maturation intermediates was impaired (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Upon Spb4 or Rrp17 depletion, the recruitment of Nop53 and downstream nucleoplasmic assembly factors such as Nog2 and Bud20 was impaired.
source: In the absence of Spb4 or Rrp17, pre-60S maturation was effectively arrested at a late nucleolar stage, as apparent by the accumulation of assembly factors Ytm1–Erb1, Spb1, and Has1 on Nug1- and Nop7-derived particles, whereas the recruitment of Nop53 and downstream nucleoplasmic assembly factors such as Nog2 and Bud20 to these stalled maturation intermediates was impaired (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Spb4 and Rrp17 have an important function for pre-60S maturation before Ytm1–Erb1 dissociation and transition of pre-60S particles to the nucleoplasm.
source: This suggests an important function of both Spb4 and Rrp17 for pre-60S maturation before Ytm1–Erb1 dissociation and transition of pre-60S particles to the nucleoplasm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the depletion experiments.

claim: Upon Spb4 or Rrp17 depletion, the export factor Arx1 failed to efficiently co-purify pre-ribosomes and was instead present mainly in a free form or associated with mature ribosomes or non-ribosomal factors.
source: Consistently, the export factor Arx1 that joins at a nucleoplasmic stage failed to efficiently co-purify pre-ribosomes upon Spb4 or Rrp17 depletion and was instead present mainly in a free form or associated with mature ribosomes or non-ribosomal factors (e.g. importins) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The association of Spb4 with Nug1- and Nop7-derived particles was a prerequisite for recruitment of Rrp17.
source: Notably, while the association of Spb4 with Nug1- and Nop7-derived particles was a prerequisite for recruitment of Rrp17, the presence of Rrp17 was apparently not strictly required for Spb4-recruitment to these 60S precursors (Figure 2B, right panel; note that in Figure 2C Spb4 is co-migrating with the Nug1-Flag bait protein as revealed by mass spectrometry analyses).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The presence of Rrp17 was apparently not strictly required for Spb4-recruitment to 60S precursors.
source: Notably, while the association of Spb4 with Nug1- and Nop7-derived particles was a prerequisite for recruitment of Rrp17, the presence of Rrp17 was apparently not strictly required for Spb4-recruitment to these 60S precursors (Figure 2B, right panel; note that in Figure 2C Spb4 is co-migrating with the Nug1-Flag bait protein as revealed by mass spectrometry analyses).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Spb4 may associate with 60S precursors shortly before Rrp17 and help to mediate its incorporation.
source: Taken together, our data revealed an essential function of Spb4 and Rrp17 during final steps of nucleolar pre-60S maturation directly prior to release of the Erb1–Ytm1 subcomplex and subsequent assembly of Nop53. Thereby, Spb4 may associate with 60S precursors shortly before Rrp17 and help to mediate its incorporation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The major class of Spb4-FTpA particles closely resembles the structural state E and was resolved at an overall resolution of 2.7 Å.
source: The major class of particles (40.85% of particles after 2D classification), which closely resembles the structural state E (Kater et al., 2017), was resolved at an overall resolution of 2.7 Å (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E)
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in the figures.

claim: A minor class of Spb4-FTpA particles corresponded to state D at an overall resolution of 3.0 Å.
source: whereas a minor class corresponded to state D at an overall resolution of 3.0 Å (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F–I).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in the figures.

claim: The state D class contains the Nsa1 module (consisting of assembly factors Nsa1, Rpf1, Mak16, and Rrp1) at the solvent-exposed pre-60S side but is otherwise identical to state E.
source: The latter class contains in addition the Nsa1 module (consisting of assembly factors Nsa1, Rpf1, Mak16, and Rrp1) at the solvent-exposed pre-60S side but is otherwise identical to the better resolved state E (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The higher resolution of the state E structure allowed identification and building of molecular models of assembly factors Spb4, Rrp17, Noc2, and Loc1, as well as additional parts of Noc3, Spb1, Nsa3, and of the ITS2 RNA.
source: The higher resolution of the state E compared to our previous study (Kater et al., 2017) allowed us to identify and build molecular models of assembly factors Spb4, Rrp17, Noc2, and Loc1, as well to resolve additional parts of Noc3, Spb1, Nsa3, and of the ITS2 RNA (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data.

claim: At the inter-subunit side Spb4 is in contact with Rrp17 and located on top of the immature rRNA helices H62 and H63 in direct vicinity to the Ytm1–Erb1 complex.
source: At the inter-subunit side Spb4 is in contact with Rrp17 and located on top of the immature rRNA helices H62 and H63 in direct vicinity to the Ytm1–Erb1 complex (Figure 3A, B, H and I).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Loc1 is located at the solvent-exposed pre-60S side where it engages in multiple protein interactions with assembly factors Noc3, Spb1, Nip7, Erb1, Ebp2, Brx1, and ribosomal protein Rpl15 (eL15).
source: The intertwined Loc1 is located at the solvent-exposed pre-60S side where it engages in multiple protein interactions with assembly factors Noc3, Spb1, Nip7, Erb1, Ebp2, Brx1, and ribosomal protein Rpl15 (eL15) (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Noc3 interacts with the C-terminal part of its heat-repeat domain with its binding partner Noc2.
source: Next to Loc1, Noc3 interacts with the C-terminal part of its heat-repeat domain with its binding partner Noc2 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The C-terminal Noc2 heat-repeat domain and the N-terminal part of the protein are visible, and both contribute to establish the interaction with Noc3.
source: While the middle part of Noc2 (aa 86–176) is not resolved, the C-terminal Noc2 heat-repeat domain and the N-terminal part of the protein are visible, and both contribute to establish the interaction with Noc3.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data.

claim: The Noc2 N-terminus protrudes deeply into the 60S core and contacts the immature H35 rRNA, which likely requires Noc2 dissociation to adopt its mature conformation.
source: Besides its interaction with Noc3, Noc2 is anchored to the particle by its elongated N-terminus that protrudes deeply into the 60S core. There, the Noc2 N-terminus contacts the immature H35 rRNA, which likely requires Noc2 dissociation to adopt its mature conformation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Additional parts of the ITS2 spacer RNA (nucleotides 60–65 and 213–226) and the C-terminus of Nsa3 (aa 324–353) were resolved at the prominent pre-60S 'foot' structure.
source: We were also able to resolve additional parts of the ITS2 spacer RNA (nucleotides 60–65 and 213–226) and the C-terminus of Nsa3 (aa 324–353) at the prominent pre-60S 'foot' structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claim: ITS2 bases 62–65 base-pair with 213–216, which is in line with a proposed 'ring-pin' model for the ITS2 structure based on chemical probing data.
source: This unveiled internal base-pairing of ITS2 bases 62–65 with 213–216, which is in line with a proposed 'ring-pin' model for the ITS2 structure based on chemical probing data (Burlacu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data and consistent with previous chemical probing data.

claim: The ITS2 RNA and Nsa3 are twined around and enclose assembly factor Nop15, which can presumably dissociate only upon ITS2 processing and subsequent release of the foot factors.
source: Furthermore, it revealed how the ITS2 RNA and Nsa3 are twined around and enclose assembly factor Nop15 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D), which therefore can presumably dissociate only upon ITS2 processing and subsequent release of the foot factors (Gasse et al., 2015; Schuller et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data and inferred from the structural arrangement, with citations to previous studies.

claim: A ligand within the binding pocket of Spb1's methyltransferase domain (MTD) is most probably S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH).
source: Notably, we identified a ligand within the binding pocket of Spb1's methyltransferase domain (MTD), which is most probably S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH) (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B)
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Methylation of Spb1's 2'-O-ribose target in nucleotide G2922 of the A-site loop has occurred at the state E stage.
source: Notably, we identified a ligand within the binding pocket of Spb1's methyltransferase domain (MTD), which is most probably S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH) (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), suggesting that methylation of its 2'-O-ribose target in nucleotide G2922 of the A-site loop (Lapeyre and Purushothaman, 2004) has occurred at this stage.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of SAH in the binding pocket, with citation to previous work identifying the target.

claim: The G2922 methylation was shown to be monitored by the GTPase Nog2 establishing a crucial checkpoint for pre-60S maturation.
source: The G2922 methylation was most recently shown to be monitored by the GTPase Nog2 establishing a crucial checkpoint for pre-60S maturation (Yelland et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study (Yelland et al., 2023).

claim: The very N-terminal part of Spb1 (aa 4–27) may play an important role for target recognition as it clamps 25S rRNA H92 that harbours nucleotide G2922 and thereby suitably positions it for methylation.
source: To facilitate this modification, the very N-terminal part of Spb1 (aa 4–27) may play an important role for target recognition as it clamps 25S rRNA H92 that harbours nucleotide G2922 and thereby suitably positions it for methylation (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM structural data showing the interaction.

claim: Gm2922 and adjacent Um2921 were observed in the corresponding RNA density.
source: In agreement with 2'-O-ribose methylation of G2922 at the analysed stage, we observed Gm2922 in the corresponding RNA density as well as adjacent Um2921 (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B)
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Um2921 is in a redundant function methylated by Spb1 or the snR52 C/D box snoRNP at an earlier pre-60S biogenesis step.
source: which is in a redundant function methylated by Spb1 or the snR52 C/D box snoRNP at an earlier pre-60S biogenesis step (Bonnerot et al., 2003; Lapeyre and Purushothaman, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Bonnerot et al., 2003; Lapeyre and Purushothaman, 2004).

claim: The α-helical Rrp17 is present at the inter-subunit side clamped between the MTD of Spb1 and the helicase core of Spb4.
source: The α-helical Rrp17 is present at the inter-subunit side clamped between the MTD of Spb1 and the helicase core of Spb4 (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The essential unstructured Rrp17 N-terminus is meandering across the MTD of Spb1.
source: While the essential unstructured Rrp17 N-terminus is meandering across the MTD of Spb1 (Figure 3D), a more central part of the protein (aa 145–159) is reaching towards Spb4 forming an anti-parallel β-sheet with the N-terminal RecA-like domain of the helicase (Figure 3I and J, Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3D, 3I, 3J, and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claim: A central part of Rrp17 (aa 145–159) forms an anti-parallel β-sheet with the N-terminal RecA-like domain of Spb4.
source: While the essential unstructured Rrp17 N-terminus is meandering across the MTD of Spb1 (Figure 3D), a more central part of the protein (aa 145–159) is reaching towards Spb4 forming an anti-parallel β-sheet with the N-terminal RecA-like domain of the helicase (Figure 3I and J, Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3I, 3J, and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Disruption of the β-sheet augmentation in rrp17 154–160>A and 154–160>R mutant cells yielded slow-growth phenotypes, revealing the importance of the Rrp17–Spb4 contact.
source: Prompted by this β-sheet augmentation, we analysed the growth of yeast cells upon mutation of the corresponding Rrp17 amino acids (154–160). As observed for N-terminal (Spb1 interaction) but not C-terminal Rrp17 truncation mutants, disruption of the β-sheet augmentation in rrp17 154–160>A and 154–160>R mutant cells yielded slow-growth phenotypes, revealing the importance of this Rrp17–Spb4 contact (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B.

claim: A yeast two-hybrid interaction between Spb4 and Rrp17 was observed, mediated by the central part of Rrp17 (aa 106–177) that includes amino acids 154–160.
source: Moreover, a yeast two-hybrid interaction between Spb4 and Rrp17 was observed, mediated by the central part of Rrp17 (aa 106–177) that includes amino acids 154–160 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5C.

claim: The C-terminal part of Rrp17 (aa 209–235) contacts the Spb1 MTD in proximity of its N-terminus, as well as 25S rRNA H64.
source: The C-terminal part of Rrp17 (aa 209–235) is reaching back and contacts again the Spb1 MTD in proximity of its N-terminus, as well as 25S rRNA H64 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Spb4 purifications contained a mixture of distinct NE1-like states downstream of Ytm1–Erb1 removal as well as state E-like particles with only weak densities for the L1 stalk, Rrp17, and the Spb1 MTD.
source: In the major class of the obtained state E-like Spb4 particles, Rrp17 and Spb1 including its N-terminal MTD were already incorporated as described above. In addition, the Spb4 purifications contained a mixture of distinct NE1-like states downstream of Ytm1–Erb1 removal (Kater et al., 2020) as well as state E-like particles with only weak densities for the L1 stalk, Rrp17, and the Spb1 MTD, potentially representing intermediates upstream of state E (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: An additional E-like state (resolved at 3.1 Å) lacking Rrp17 and Spb1 MTD densities but showing stable incorporation of the L1 stalk may represent a novel maturation intermediate directly preceding state E.
source: Moreover, analysis of another independent dataset of purified Spb4 particles, which underwent an only partially efficient maturation reaction, revealed an additional E-like state (resolved at 3.1 Å) lacking the corresponding Rrp17 and Spb1 MTD densities but show stable incorporation of the L1 stalk (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2J–M, Figure 3—figure supplement 6). We conclude that this state may indeed represent a novel maturation intermediate directly preceding state E.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data and inferred from the structural features.

claim: Spb4 is assembled around state D/E shortly prior to final Spb1 MTD and Rrp17 incorporation.
source: Taken together, our cryo-EM analyses suggest that Spb4 is assembled around state D/E shortly prior to final Spb1 MTD and Rrp17 incorporation, which agrees with the biochemical protein data of purified pre-60S particles upon Spb4 and Rrp17 depletion (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cryo-EM structural data and biochemical data.

claim: A single-stranded rRNA (nucleotides U1942 to A1945 of 25S rRNA H63) is observed within the Spb4 helicase core active site.
source: Most importantly, we observe a single-stranded rRNA (nucleotides U1942 to A1945 of 25S rRNA H63) within the helicase core active site (Figure 3K, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The accommodation of the rRNA substrate between the two RecA-like domains induces bending and strand separation of the rRNA around the base of ES27, resulting in an alternate base-pairing of helices H62/H63/H63a compared to nucleoplasmic maturation intermediates and mature 60S subunits.
source: The accommodation of the rRNA substrate between the two RecA-like domains induces bending and strand separation of the rRNA around the base of ES27, resulting in an alternate base-pairing of helices H62/H63/H63a compared to nucleoplasmic maturation intermediates and mature 60S subunits (Figure 3C and K).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3C and 3K.

claim: The rRNA area at the base of 25S domain IV initially appears to form stable duplexes, while it becomes more flexible and accessible for chemical modification in presence of Spb4.
source: This may explain why the rRNA area at the base of 25S domain IV initially appears to form stable duplexes, while it becomes more flexible and accessible for chemical modification in presence of Spb4, suggesting that the helicase disrupts this region upon its association (Brüning et al., 2018; Burlacu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and supported by citations to previous chemical probing studies.

claim: Spb4's essential CTD is significantly involved in inducing substrate RNA strand disruption and establishing the alternate conformation.
source: In addition to the catalytic domain, Spb4's essential CTD appears significantly involved in inducing substrate RNA strand disruption and establishing this alternate conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing CTD interactions with the rRNA.

claim: The first half of the Spb4 CTD (aa 406–499) is tightly docked onto the C-terminal RecA-like domain (RecA2) and binds H62/H63 nucleotides A1936 to C1941, thereby maintaining separation of the rRNA strands.
source: In the obtained substrate-bound state, the first half of the CTD (aa 406–499) is tightly docked onto the C-terminal RecA-like domain (RecA2) and binds H62/H63 nucleotides A1936 to C1941, thereby maintaining separation of the rRNA strands (Figure 3C, K and L, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3C, 3K, 3L, and Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: A conserved tryptophan (W536) within the flexible C-terminal tail of the Spb4 CTD (aa 500–606) intercalates between nucleotides of the immature H62/H63/H63a rRNA.
source: Furthermore, a conserved tryptophan (W536) within the flexible C-terminal tail of the CTD (aa 500–606) intercalates between nucleotides of the immature H62/H63/H63a rRNA, which later adopts its mature-like fold in nucleoplasmic pre-60S particles (Figure 3C and L).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3C and 3L.

claim: Spb4 accommodates ADP in its binding pocket while the two RecA domains are in a closed conformation and tightly bound to the substrate RNA.
source: Examination of the catalytic Spb4 core in our structure revealed that, while the two RecA domains are in a clear closed conformation and tightly bound to the substrate RNA, the helicase surprisingly accommodates in its binding pocket a nucleotide which we could unambiguously identify as ADP (Figure 3M, Figure 3—figure supplement 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3M and Figure 3—figure supplement 4D and E.

claim: Spb4 has already hydrolysed ATP at a previous step but remains associated with pre-ribosomes in a post-catalytic and still ADP-bound closed state.
source: Thus, Spb4 has already hydrolysed ATP at a previous step but remains associated with pre-ribosomes in a post-catalytic and still ADP-bound closed state and preserves its re-arranged rRNA substrate in the observed immature alternate conformation as also observed in a recent structure (Cruz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing ADP in the closed conformation, and consistent with a recent study.

claim: ATP binding and hydrolysis provide the energy for binding and local strand melting of the rRNA which is then followed by a subsequent stabilization of this state through the observed interactions of Sbp4 with several assembly factors such as Rrp17.
source: This unusual behaviour can be explained by the requirement of ATP binding and hydrolysis to provide the energy for binding and local strand melting of the rRNA which is then followed by a subsequent stabilization of this state through the observed interactions of Sbp4 with several assembly factors such as Rrp17.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation inferred from the structural data.

claim: The interaction and activity of Sbp4 appears to set the stage for the correct formation of the H61-H62-H63-H64 rRNA region as an important prerequisite for the further maturation of rRNA domain IV.
source: Thus, the interaction and activity of Sbp4 appears to set the stage for the correct formation of the H61-H62-H63-H64 rRNA region as an important prerequisite for the further maturation of rRNA domain IV.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and functional data.

claim: Incubation of Ytm1-derived particles with purified Rea1, the pentameric Rix-complex, and ATP did not result in release of the Ytm1–Erb1 complex.
source: We incubated Ytm1-derived particles with affinity purified Rea1, the pentameric Rix-complex (i.e. Rix12–Ipi32–Ipi1; this complex is suggested to guide Rea1 to its pre-ribosomal substrates), and ATP. However, upon subsequent re-isolation of pre-60S particles via Rpl3-Flag, the Ytm1–Erb1 complex remained fully associated with the pre-ribosomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Performing the maturation assay with Spb4-purified pre-60S particles exhibited an efficient release of the Ytm1–Erb1 complex and the DEAD-box helicase Has1.
source: Strikingly, performing this maturation assay with Spb4-purified pre-60S particles exhibited an efficient release of the Ytm1–Erb1 complex and, remarkably, the DEAD-box helicase Has1 (Figure 4A, lane 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The release of Ytm1–Erb1 and Has1 was more efficient in presence of the Rix1-complex, however, the addition of Rea1 and ATP was in principle sufficient to perform the restructuring step.
source: The release of these assembly factors was more efficient in presence of the Rix1-complex, however, the addition of Rea1 and ATP was in principle sufficient to perform the restructuring step, at least in this in vitro setup with excess of purified Rea1 (Figure 4A, lane 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The in vitro maturation occurred when the slow growing catalytic spb4 R360A mutant was used, indicating that ATP-hydrolysis by Spb4 is not required for this maturation step.
source: The in vitro maturation also occurred when the slow growing catalytic spb4 R360A mutant was used (Figure 1C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and D), which indicates that ATP-hydrolysis by Spb4 is not required for this maturation step.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and D.

claim: Pre-60S recruitment of Spb4 and potentially also Rrp17 is a prerequisite for Rea1-dependent remodelling.
source: However, since in vitro maturation was inducible on Spb4- but not on Ytm1-derived pre-60S particles that co-purify only small amounts of the helicase Spb4 (Figure 1A), we conclude that pre-60S recruitment of Spb4 and potentially also Rrp17 is a prerequisite for this remodelling step.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro maturation experiments.

claim: Incubation of Rrp17 particles with Rea1, Rix1-complex, and ATP resulted in limited but clearly detectable release of the sub-stoichiometrically associated Ytm1–Erb1 complex.
source: Indeed, also incubation of Rrp17 particles with Rea1, Rix1-complex, and ATP resulted in limited but clearly detectable release of the sub-stoichiometrically associated Ytm1–Erb1 complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Has1 is bound at the top of the foot and is contacted by the meandering unstructured Erb1 N-terminal tail.
source: While Rea1's direct substrate Ytm1 is recruited to the pre-60S subunit via tight interactions with the C-terminal β-propeller domain of Erb1 near the bottom of the foot-structure (Kater et al., 2017; Thoms et al., 2016; Wegrecki et al., 2015), the RNA helicase Has1 is bound at a distant site over H16 at the top of the foot and is contacted by the meandering unstructured Erb1 N-terminal tail (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A; Kater et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and citations to previous studies.

claim: The nucleotide binding pocket of Has1 was found empty in the pre-60S cryo-EM structure.
source: The nucleotide binding pocket of Has1 was found empty in our and a previously published pre-60S cryo-EM structure (Zhou et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data and citation to a previous study.

claim: Wild-type and mutant Has1 proteins were released with similar efficiency together with the Ytm1–Erb1 complex, demonstrating that the removal of all three factors occurs independently from Has1's catalytic activity.
source: Upon incubation with Rea1, the Rix1-complex, and ATP, wild-type and mutant Has1 proteins were released with similar efficiency together with the Ytm1–Erb1 complex, demonstrating that the removal of all three factors occurs independently from Has1's catalytic activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, left panel; compare lanes 4 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The Ytm1–Erb1 release could be induced from particles in absence of any Has1 protein.
source: Furthermore, the Ytm1–Erb1 release could be induced also from particles in absence of any Has1 protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, right panel; lane 12).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The Rea1-dependent pre-60S release of the Ytm1–Erb1 complex occurs before and independently of Has1, and in turn results in displacement of the helicase.
source: Thus, the Rea1-dependent pre-60S release of the Ytm1–Erb1 complex occurs before and independently of Has1, and in turn results in displacement of the helicase, which is potentially pulled off by its interaction with the intertwined Erb1 tail.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Rea1/Rix1-complex/ATP-induced remodelling of Spb4 particles in vitro resulted in maturation from E-like to distinct NE1-like states.
source: We conclude that Rea1/Rix1-complex/ATP-induced remodelling of Spb4 particles in vitro resulted in maturation from E-like to distinct NE1-like states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cryo-EM analysis of in vitro matured particles.

claim: All three release states have strong resemblance to the previously described NE1 state but lack the foot-factor Nop53.
source: All three release states have strong resemblance to the previously described NE1 state (obtained from Nop53 affinity purifications) but lack the foot-factor Nop53.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural comparison.

claim: A minor particle class containing Nop53 indicates that the attachment of Spb4 and Nop53 to pre-60S intermediates might not be strictly mutually exclusive.
source: However, we also find a minor particle class containing Nop53, which indicates that the attachment of Spb4 and Nop53 to pre-60S intermediates might not be strictly mutually exclusive (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: All obtained release state particles still contain Rrp17 bound to the Spb1 MTD.
source: Notably, all obtained release state particles still contain Rrp17 bound to the Spb1 MTD (Figure 4B and C), which is in line with Rrp17-FTpA purifications suggesting that the protein is still present on intermediates downstream of Spb4 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 4B and 4C, and consistent with biochemical data in Figure 1D.

claim: The Ytm1–Erb1 complex, the helicase Has1 and also Spb4 were no longer visible in the in vitro released states.
source: In contrast, the Ytm1–Erb1 complex, the helicase Has1 and also Spb4 were no longer visible in the in vitro released states.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data.

claim: Spb4 remained attached to the in vitro matured pre-60S particles in a flexible way and hence was not detectible by cryo-EM.
source: Since Spb4 was our bait for specimen purification, it appears that Spb4 remained attached to the in vitro matured pre-60S particles in a flexible way and hence was not detectible by cryo-EM.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that Spb4 was the bait but not visible in the structures.

claim: One of the released states showed a fuzzy density in the area where the Spb4 helicase core is located in the preceding state E, and rigid body fitting suggests that the poorly resolved density corresponds to Spb4.
source: Indeed, one of the released states showed a fuzzy density in the area where the Spb4 helicase core is located in the preceding state E, and rigid body fitting of the Spb4 helicase core clearly suggests that the poorly resolved density corresponds to Spb4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6B.

claim: The densities for several assembly factors such as Loc1, Brx1, Ebp2, Noc2–Noc3, Nip7, Nop2 at the inter-subunit side, and Nop16 at the solvent-exposed side were not visible in the released NE1-like particles, revealing large-scale remodelling.
source: Moreover, the densities for several other assembly factors such as Loc1, Brx1, Ebp2, Noc2–Noc3, Nip7, Nop2 at the inter-subunit side, and Nop16 at the solvent-exposed side were not visible in the released NE1-like particles, revealing large-scale remodelling around the area that in state E is accessed and connected by the long N-terminal Erb1 tail (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Erb1 removal could result in destabilization of these factors, which may become invisible either by complete removal or flexible attachment to the in vitro matured pre-60S particles.
source: Thus, Erb1 removal could result in destabilization of these factors, which may become invisible either by complete removal or flexible attachment to the in vitro matured pre-60S particles.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation inferred from the structural data.

claim: Induction of the ATP-dependent release of the Ytm1–Erb1 heterodimer by the AAA+-ATPase Rea1 results in large-scale remodelling of pre-60S particles isolated via the RNA helicase Spb4.
source: By combining biochemical and structural cryo-EM analyses, we unveiled how induction of the ATP-dependent release of the Ytm1–Erb1 heterodimer by the AAA+-ATPase Rea1 results in large-scale remodelling of pre-60S particles isolated via the RNA helicase Spb4.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: In vitro matured particles, from which a network of assembly factors appeared dismantled, with subtle variations, resembled structural state NE1, while largely lacking assembly factor Nop53.
source: Such in vitro matured particles, from which a network of assembly factors appeared dismantled, with subtle variations, resembled structural state NE1, while largely lacking assembly factor Nop53.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data.

claim: NE1 is the earliest state obtained upon purification of native pre-60S particles isolated via Nop53, which can only join upon release of Erb1 due to overlapping binding sites at the pre-60S foot structure.
source: NE1 is the earliest state obtained upon purification of native pre-60S particles isolated via Nop53, which can only join upon release of Erb1 due to overlapping binding sites at the pre-60S foot structure (Kater et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study (Kater et al., 2020).

claim: The initial release of Ytm1–Erb1 and Has1 may result in pre-rRNA re-arrangement and assembly factor destabilization, which would in consequence be too flexible to be resolved by cryo-EM or become unstably attached and potentially dissociate during cryo-EM sample preparation.
source: The initial release of Ytm1–Erb1 and Has1 may therefore result in pre-rRNA re-arrangement and assembly factor destabilization, which would in consequence be too flexible to be resolved by cryo-EM or become unstably attached and potentially dissociate during cryo-EM sample preparation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for the observed structural changes.

claim: It remains open whether in vivo further factors and intermediary maturation steps are required to facilitate assembly factor disassembly and formation of NE1 particles upon Ytm1–Erb1 and Has1 release.
source: However, it remains open whether in vivo further factors and intermediary maturation steps are required to facilitate assembly factor disassembly and formation of NE1 particles upon Ytm1–Erb1 and Has1 release.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitations of the in vitro system and the need for further investigation.

claim: Has1 dissociates in an ATP-independent manner from 60S precursors.
source: As furthermore a Has1 Walker A mutant protein was efficiently released from the particle in our maturation assay, we conclude that Has1 dissociates in an ATP-independent manner from 60S precursors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with the Has1 mutant.

claim: The role of Has1 in pre-60S maturation could be ATP-independent and may depend only on its physical presence.
source: This is in agreement with previous studies suggesting that the Has1 function on 90S pre-ribosomes requires its catalytic activity (Gnanasundram et al., 2019; Liang and Fournier, 2006), while the role of Has1 in pre-60S maturation could be ATP-independent and may depend only on its physical presence (Gnanasundram et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Has1's catalytic activity may be required during its initial pre-60S recruitment on early nucleolar precursors.
source: Alternatively, since Has1 binds already to very early nucleolar pre-60S maturation intermediates, its catalytic activity may be required during its initial pre-60S recruitment.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation.

claim: Has1 was implicated to play a role for contact formation between the 25S 5' end and the 5.8S rRNA on early nucleolar precursors.
source: On such early nucleolar precursors, Has1 was implicated to play a role for contact formation between the 25S 5' end and the 5.8S rRNA (Dembowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study (Dembowski et al., 2013).

claim: The pentameric Rix1-complex recruits the AAA+-ATPase Rea1 to nucleoplasmic pre-60S particles before nuclear export.
source: Our previous cryo-EM structures of nucleoplasmic pre-60S particles revealed how the pentameric Rix1-complex recruits the AAA+-ATPase Rea1 to these intermediates before nuclear export (Barrio-Garcia et al., 2016; Kater et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies by the authors.

claim: The Rix1-complex is essential to accurately position Rea1 for interaction and the subsequent release of its direct substrate Rsa4.
source: The Rix1-complex is thereby essential to accurately position Rea1 for interaction and the subsequent release of its direct substrate Rsa4.
evidence: This is supported by previous structural studies.

claim: The Rix1-complex recruits Rea1 to its earlier pre-60S substrate as well.
source: Previous results (Bassler et al., 2010) and the increased efficiency in Ytm1–Erb1 release contributed by the Rix1-complex in our in vitro maturation assays suggest that the Rix1-complex recruits Rea1 to its earlier pre-60S substrate as well.
evidence: This is inferred from previous results and the current in vitro maturation data.

claim: It remains unclear how the ATPase extracts Ytm1–Erb1 and how the Rix1-complex mediates this remodelling step.
source: Nevertheless, since structural insights into the more transient interaction of Rea1 with these nucleolar 60S precursors are missing, it remains unclear how the ATPase extracts Ytm1–Erb1 and how the Rix1-complex mediates this remodelling step.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitations of the current study.

claim: The DEAH helicase Dhr1 and the Ski2-like helicase Mtr4 unwind the U3 snoRNA and RNA spacer substrates, respectively.
source: Two exceptions in which ribosome-bound helicase structures could be determined are the DEAH helicase Dhr1 and the Ski2-like helicase Mtr4, which unwind the U3 snoRNA and RNA spacer substrates, respectively (Cheng et al., 2020; Du et al., 2020; Lau et al., 2021; Schuller et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: DEAD-box helicases are proposed to mediate RNA folding by non-processive local strand melting and annealing.
source: In contrast to such processive helicases, DEAD-box helicases are proposed to mediate RNA folding by non-processive local strand melting and annealing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DEAD-box helicase mechanisms.

claim: The existing general model on the function of DEAD-box helicases suggests that substrate RNA and ATP-binding together induce the closed active conformation of the catalytic RecA domains, whereas ATP-hydrolysis in the active site instantly triggers a re-opening of the catalytic domains going along with the release of the restructured RNA substrate.
source: The existing general model on the function of DEAD-box helicases suggests that substrate RNA and ATP-binding together induce the closed active conformation of the catalytic RecA domains, whereas ATP-hydrolysis in the active site instantly triggers a re-opening of the catalytic domains going along with the release of the restructured RNA substrate.(Andersen et al., 2006; Bono et al., 2006; Mallam et al., 2012; Sengoku et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DEAD-box helicase mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Current models on the function of DEAD-box helicases need to be extended since on complex substrates such as pre-ribosomes several additional factors might influence the state of the catalytic domains.
source: We therefore assume that current models on the function of DEAD-box helicases need to be extended since on complex substrates such as pre-ribosomes several additional factors might influence the state of the catalytic domains.
